extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, Federal Circuit practitioners, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Federal Circuit doctrinal standards and evidentiary criteria for patent litigation topics (obviousness, claim construction, infringement doctrines, defenses, ITC domestic industry, and Hatch‑Waxman/§271(e)(1)). Useful guidance for litigating or evaluating patent disputes under recent Federal Circuit precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine prior art for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A skilled artisan must have a reason or motivation to combine prior art references; the mere fact that different approaches or coordinate systems were known in the prior art is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit reversed a PTAB finding where neither the prior art nor the petition provided any reason why a POSA would use 3D coordinates instead of angular directions. Courts require an articulated motivation to combine; substitution known in the art does not alone prove obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive/common-sense assertions insufficient to prove motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of obviousness cannot rest on conclusory testimony that elements are 'well-known' or on an assertion that combination is justified by 'common sense' without evidentiary support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalized or conclusory expert testimony that elements were known or that a combination is 'common sense' is inadequate. The patentee/accuser must provide nonconclusory evidence showing why a POSA would combine the references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of interrelated teachings and POSA creativity (KSR compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness analysis must give needed weight to the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA), including their ability to deduce what references fairly suggest and their ordinary creativity; courts must consider the interrelated teachings of references and background knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should not be 'impermissibly rigid' by ignoring how a POSA might combine references using ordinary creativity. Avoid premature rejection of combinations because a reference lacks specific results or stated safety/efficacy data if a POSA could nonetheless find it obvious to modify protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success in obviousness combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining references to show obviousness, a skilled artisan must have had a reasonable expectation of success in achieving the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pharmaceutical/dosage cases, courts evaluate the combined message of prior art (e.g., teaching that an optimal dose may be higher) and whether that would lead a POSA to a dosage with a reasonable expectation of success. Evidence that prior art suggested higher dosing and available dosage increments can support obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art statement 'teaches away' only when it explicitly discourages the claimed modification or values, not when it merely recommends a preferred or optimal value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preferred value in a reference (e.g., an optimal particle size) does not constitute teaching away unless the prior art disparages or directs away from other values. Courts must distinguish preference from discouragement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia such as commercial success, long‑felt need, industry praise, copying, and licensing are relevant to the obviousness inquiry and must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial courts/juries should be instructed to consider all relevant objective indicia presented (e.g., industry praise, copying, licensing activity) as they may cut against a finding of obviousness. Omitting asserted objective indicia from jury instructions can be prejudicial and reversible error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of combining known elements to render discovery nonobvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifying or characterizing information about a substance previously known in the art by combining known elements does not necessarily render the discovery nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery of a previously-unknown property or form that can be obtained by routine application of known techniques to known substances may be held obvious where the skilled artisan had ability and motivation to perform the characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting (OTDP) & patent term adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: OTDP prevents patentees from obtaining a second patent on a patentably indistinct invention to effectively extend the life of the first patent; the first‑filed, first‑issued patent in a family sets the maximum exclusivity period for claimed subject matter and variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will consider whether continuing patents improperly extend rights beyond the first‑filed/first‑issued family's maximum exclusivity, including issues arising from patent term adjustments (PTA). Distinguish prior precedent where additional PTA in continuations was treated as extending term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: do not read limitations into claims absent support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be construed to include limitations not present in the claim language unless the intrinsic record clearly compels it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims reciting 'a psychiatric patient' were improperly read to require suitability for the 'general population.' Courts must base constructions on claim language and intrinsic evidence, avoiding importation of unclaimed limitations such as specific patient subgroups (e.g., 'mild renal impairment') unless clearly required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction of numeric values and rounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric claim language (e.g., 'a pH of 13 or higher') can be ambiguous as to rounding and approximation, and may require extrinsic evidence to resolve whether conventional margins of error apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where specification and prosecution history are inconclusive about whether a numeric value allows rounding (e.g., whether '13' means 12.5–13.4), courts may seek extrinsic evidence (textbook excerpts, expert testimony) to determine the proper construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad interpretation of 'based at least in part on' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'based at least in part on' place no constraint on the manner in which inputs are used unless the specification imposes such a constraint; inputs need not be used distinctly from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The broadest reasonable interpretation permits an input to be calculated from another claimed input. Absent intrinsic language limiting the manner of use, do not treat listed inputs as required to be independent components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification statements describing 'the invention' can limit claims when uniform
rubrics_metrics.description: When the specification uniformly refers to an aspect (e.g., pre-fetching) as part of 'this invention' or 'the method,' that description can inform a limiting claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although references to 'the invention' are not always limiting, where the intrinsic evidence and prosecution history uniformly tie an embodiment (such as pre‑fetching advertising objects) to the invention, courts may construe the claims to include that aspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction on motion to dismiss — scope and need for fuller proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may perform claim construction on a motion to dismiss when based on intrinsic evidence alone, but some cases require fuller claim‑construction proceedings, extrinsic evidence, or expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where intrinsic evidence suggests multiple plausible constructions or the record is limited (e.g., interpretation of 'group' as 'one or more'), courts should recognize circumstances where dismissal‑stage construction is inappropriate and remand for more complete proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — particularized testimony and linking argument required
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof under the doctrine of equivalents must include 'particularized testimony and linking argument' showing insubstantial differences between claimed elements and accused device features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts or other evidence must identify specific elements in the accused product that correspond to claim limitations, explain how the function, way, and result are equivalent, and connect that analysis to the claim language. Generalized testimony is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — means‑way‑result and insubstantial differences analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the means‑way‑result framework and the insubstantial differences approach, a patentee must show equivalence in function, way, and result, and explain why any differences are insubstantial in light of what the claim avoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should address each prong (function, way, result) with specifics. Demonstrations that the accused product performs the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result are required; unsupported generalizations fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — form of admissible evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of equivalents must be from the perspective of someone skilled in the art and can include expert testimony, documents (texts, treatises), and prior art disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court rejected creating an exception based on technological simplicity: even 'simple' technologies require particularized linking evidence. The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit expect POSA‑oriented evidence rather than lay or conclusory statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducement to infringe — specific intent and action required
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove inducement, the plaintiff must show that the defendant had specific intent to induce infringement and took actions to induce it; mere knowledge that infringement will occur is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Hatch‑Waxman/ANDA contexts, labels that carve out patented uses and otherwise comply with regulatory requirements weigh against intent to induce. Evidence that clinicians might independently prescribe for patented uses does not establish defendant's intent or actions to induce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatch‑Waxman label carve‑outs reduce inducement risk
rubrics_metrics.description: An ANDA applicant's removal of references to patented patient classes or uses from its label (carve‑outs) demonstrates an attempt to avoid encouraging infringing uses and undermines inducement claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will consider whether the label explicitly encourages or recommends infringing uses. Properly tailored labels that omit patented indications make inducement less likely to be proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: §271(e)(1) safe harbor scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities 'solely for uses reasonably related to the development and submission of information' to the FDA fall within §271(e)(1)'s safe harbor, shielding otherwise infringing acts, and the safe harbor applies regardless of the actor's subjective intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts interpret 'reasonably related' broadly; acts like importing samples for use in obtaining FDA premarket approval are protected even if motivated in part by commercial considerations. The statute does not require that the 'uses reasonably related' be patent‑infringement 'uses' in the traditional sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: ITC Section 337 domestic industry requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a Section 337 violation, a complainant must show a domestic industry 'relating to the articles protected by the patent' exists or is being established, by demonstrating significant domestic investment in plant/equipment, significant employment of labor/capital, or substantial investment in exploitation (engineering, R&D, licensing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a complainant's products practice different patents or product groups, the complainant must establish separate domestic-industry showings for each group/patent and allocate its investments to each asserted patent so the Commission can evaluate significance per patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: License defense and affiliates
rubrics_metrics.description: A license defense may extend to affiliates of a licensee under state law exceptions, potentially allowing a defendant to assert a license defense when ownership/control relationships change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a non‑party affiliate is bound by a contract depends on applicable state law and recognized exceptions; courts should not summarily deny leave to assert such defenses if exceptions could make the defense viable. Futility determinations require careful analysis of controlling state precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct — Therasense standard (materiality + intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct requires clear and convincing evidence that the applicant misrepresented or omitted material information with specific intent to deceive the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must analyze materiality and intent as separate inquiries. Evidence of communications, nonresponses, or omissions must be probative of the applicant's intent at the relevant time; ambiguity or innocent explanations may defeat the required deceptive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct — pattern and egregiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern of related misconduct can, in aggregate, demonstrate deceptive intent even if individual acts do not; 'affirmative egregious misconduct' may satisfy materiality automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should consider the cumulative effect of multiple misrepresentations/omissions when assessing intent. Failure to analyze materiality separately from intent or to consider aggregate conduct can warrant reversal and remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclean hands defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The equitable doctrine of unclean hands can bar relief where a litigant engaged in deceitful, evasive, or reprehensible conduct closely connected to the claims being litigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will find unclean hands when misconduct is unconscionable and bears an immediate and necessary connection to the litigation; such a finding can preclude a party from obtaining equitable relief against an adversary.
